title: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
summary: Why wall clocks misorder events, how Lamport and vector clocks capture happened-before, and how hybrid logical clocks keep causal order within the clock skew of real time, as CockroachDB does.
outcomes: Explain why skewed wall clocks lose writes under last write wins and define happened-before precisely
Compute Lamport and vector timestamps for a message trace and say which pairs are concurrent
Apply the HLC send and receive rules to compute (l, c) timestamps and explain why c stays small
Explain how CockroachDB combines HLC with a max clock offset and uncertainty restarts, versus Spanner's commit wait

lessons.title: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines

blocks.md:
Every server has a clock, so the obvious way to order events in a distributed system is to stamp each one with the local time and sort. Databases do this to decide which of two writes to the same key is newer, and logs do it to reconstruct what happened during an outage.

The trouble is that no two clocks agree. **Clock skew** is the difference between two clocks at the same instant. Clocks also **drift**: a quartz crystal runs slightly fast or slow. Lamport's 1978 paper assumes a rate error of at most about $10^{-6}$ for crystal clocks, which on its own adds up to $86.4$ ms per day if nothing corrects it.

Machines correct drift with the **Network Time Protocol (NTP)**. The HLC paper notes NTP usually keeps clocks within tens of milliseconds over the public Internet and about one millisecond on a well-behaved LAN, but asymmetric routes and congestion can cause errors of 100 ms or more.

Corrections themselves cause surprises. Kleppmann's Cambridge notes describe the defaults: an NTP client **slews** (gently speeds up or slows down) the clock for offsets under 125 ms, **steps** it (jumps it, possibly backwards) for larger offsets, and gives up entirely beyond 1000 s. Leap seconds add more jumps.

blocks.title: Last write wins with a fast clock loses the newer write

scenes.caption: At true time 100 ms the client writes x=1 through node A. A's clock runs 30 ms fast, so A stamps the write 130.
A acknowledges. The client now knows x=1 is stored, so anything it does next is causally after this write.
At true time 110 ms the client overwrites x through node B, whose clock is correct. B stamps the newer write 110.
The replicas exchange versions and keep the larger timestamp. 130 > 110, so both keep x=1: the client's later write silently disappears.

blocks.prompt: Before the last scene: the client wrote x=1, got an OK, then wrote x=2. The replicas resolve conflicts by keeping the write with the larger timestamp (last write wins). Which value survives?
blocks.reveal: **x=1 survives**, even though x=2 was written later and the client had already seen x=1 succeed. Node A stamped its write 130 because its clock was 30 ms fast, and node B stamped the newer write 110. Last write wins compares timestamps, not causality, so a skewed clock turns into lost data with no error reported. Kyle Kingsbury's post *The trouble with timestamps* analyzes how this plays out in Cassandra and in Riak's last-write-wins mode.

scenes.caption: Each row is one node; events on a row run left to right in local order. Arrows between rows are messages m1 (A to B) and m2 (B to C). This run is used for the rest of the course.
a1 happened before c2: follow a1 to a2 (same node), a2 to b1 (message), b1 to b2 (same node), b2 to c2 (message). Information from a1 can reach c2.
a3 and b2 are concurrent: no path of arrows leads from one to the other. Neither could have influenced the other, whatever the wall clocks said.
c1 and a2 are also concurrent even though c1 sits further left in the picture. Position on a drawing, like a wall-clock reading, says nothing about causality.

blocks.md: Happened-before means *information could have flowed* from a to b through process order and messages. It is a partial order: many pairs of events are simply concurrent, and no clock reading can change that.

A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

blocks.question: In the three-node run, which pair of events is related by happened-before?
options: a3 and c2, because a3 is on A, which started the chain
c1 and c2, because they are on the same node and c1 comes first
a3 and b2, because both happen late in the run
c1 and a2, because c1 is drawn to the left of a2
blocks.explain: c1 and c2 are on the same process with c1 first, so rule 1 gives c1 happened before c2. There is no message path from a3 to anything, so a3 is concurrent with b2 and c2. c1 and a2 are concurrent too: being drawn further left is not causality.

blocks.question: A team proposes fixing the lost write by running NTP more often so clocks stay within 1 ms. What is the remaining problem?
options: None: with 1 ms skew last write wins is always correct
NTP cannot run more often than once per hour
Two causally ordered writes less than the skew apart can still get reversed timestamps, and NTP can still step a clock
Last write wins only fails when clocks run slow, never fast
blocks.explain: Tighter sync shrinks the window but does not close it. Any two causally related writes closer together than the current skew can be misordered, and NTP gives no hard guarantee: the paper cites occasional errors of 100 ms or more, and stepping can move a clock backwards.

lessons.title: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before

blocks.md: Lamport's idea is to stop measuring time and count instead. Each process $P_i$ keeps an integer register $C_i$, and every event gets the value of that register as its timestamp. The goal is the **Clock Condition**: if $a \to b$ then $C(a) < C(b)$.

blocks.caption: The Clock Condition. Lamport notes the converse cannot be required: it would force every pair of concurrent events to share a timestamp.

blocks.md:
Two implementation rules from the paper guarantee it:

- **IR1.** Each process increments $C_i$ between any two successive events.
- **IR2.** A message $m$ sent at event $a$ carries timestamp $T_m = C_i(a)$. On receipt, the process sets $C_j$ greater than or equal to its present value and greater than $T_m$.

The common way to write IR2 in code, used in Kleppmann's notes, is `t = max(t, t_msg) + 1`.

blocks.caption: A complete Lamport clock. One integer per process, one integer per message.

blocks.title: Lamport timestamps for the three-node run

scenes.caption: All three counters start at 0. Each row holds the timestamps of that node's events in local order; a dash marks an unused slot.
a1 is a local event on A: increment, so L(a1) = 1.
c1 is a local event on C: C's counter also goes from 0 to 1. Two unrelated events now share timestamp 1.
a2 sends m1: A increments to 2 and attaches 2 to the message.
b1 receives m1 carrying 2. B sets its counter to max(0, 2) + 1 = 3, so the receive is later than the send.
a3 is local on A: 2 + 1 = 3. It ties with b1, although the two events are concurrent.
b2 sends m2: B increments 3 to 4 and attaches 4.
c2 receives m2 carrying 4. C sets max(1, 4) + 1 = 5. Every happened-before edge in the run now goes from a smaller to a larger number.

blocks.prompt: In the run above, L(a3) = 3 and L(b2) = 4. Does that mean a3 happened before b2?
blocks.reveal: **No.** The diagram from lesson 1 showed a3 and b2 are concurrent: no message leaves A after a2. The Clock Condition only works one way. If $a \to b$ then $L(a) < L(b)$, so a smaller timestamp tells you $b \not\to a$, but it cannot tell you whether $a \to b$ or $a \parallel b$.

blocks.md: Lamport timestamps can tie (b1 and a3 both have 3). To get a **total order**, break ties with any fixed order on process ids. Lamport defines $a \Rightarrow b$ if $C(a) < C(b)$, or the timestamps are equal and $a$'s process comes first. This total order extends happened-before, which is exactly what replicas need to agree on one sequence of operations. Lamport used it to build a distributed mutual exclusion algorithm that grants the resource to requests in this total order.

blocks.tex: a \Rightarrow b \iff C(a) < C(b) \;\lor\; \big(C(a) = C(b) \land P(a) < P(b)\big)
blocks.caption: With A before B in the process order, (3, A) for a3 sorts before (3, B) for b1.

blocks.md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

Lamport also pointed out an **anomaly**. A user issues request A on one computer, then phones a friend who issues request B on another. The phone call is outside the system, so B can get a smaller timestamp than A and be ordered first. Lamport gives two fixes: the user can pass request A's timestamp to the friend so B is stamped later, or the system can use physical clocks synchronized well enough to satisfy the paper's Strong Clock Condition. The second motivated the physical-clock half of the paper and, decades later, hybrid clocks.

blocks.question: A node's Lamport counter is 7. It receives a message stamped 4. What timestamp does the receive event get (using t = max(t, t_msg) + 1)?
blocks.explain: max(7, 4) + 1 = 8. The receive must be later than both the node's previous event (7) and the send (4). Answer 5 would put the receive before the node's own earlier event, breaking IR1. Answer 12 adds instead of taking the max.

blocks.question: Two events have Lamport timestamps L(x) = 5 and L(y) = 9. Which conclusion is valid?
options: x happened before y
y did not happen before x
x and y are concurrent
x happened about 4 ms before y
blocks.explain: If y happened before x, the Clock Condition would force L(y) < L(x), which is false. That is all you can conclude: x may have happened before y, or they may be concurrent. Lamport timestamps have no unit of time.

blocks.md: Lamport clocks lose information because one integer cannot say *which* processes contributed to it. **Vector clocks**, proposed independently by Fidge (1988) and Mattern (1989), keep one counter per process. For $n$ nodes, a vector timestamp is $\langle t_1, \ldots, t_n \rangle$, where $t_i$ is the number of events at node $i$ that this event depends on.

The rules mirror Lamport's:

- On any event at node $i$, increment your own entry $T[i]$.
- Attach the whole vector to each message.
- On receive, take the element-wise maximum of your vector and the message's vector, then increment $T[i]$.

blocks.caption: Vector clock for node i of n.

blocks.title: Vector timestamps for the same run

scenes.caption: Each node starts with the vector [0,0,0], one entry per node in the order A, B, C.
a1 on A: increment A's own entry. [1,0,0] means one event from A is known.
c1 on C: increment C's entry to get [0,0,1].
a2 sends m1: [2,0,0] travels with the message.
b1 receives [2,0,0]: take the element-wise max with [0,0,0], then increment B's entry: [2,1,0]. B now knows A's first two events.
a3 on A: [3,0,0]. Compare with B's entries later: A's entry is larger here, B's entry is larger there.
b2 sends m2 with [2,2,0].
c2 merges [2,2,0] into [0,0,1] to get [2,2,1], then increments its own entry: [2,2,2]. The vector lists exactly how many events of each node c2 depends on.

blocks.md: Compare vectors entry by entry. $T \le T'$ if every entry of $T$ is at most the matching entry of $T'$. $T < T'$ if $T \le T'$ and they differ. If neither $T \le T'$ nor $T' \le T$, the vectors are **incomparable**. Kleppmann's notes state the payoff:

blocks.tex: V(a) < V(b) \iff a \to b \qquad V(a) \parallel V(b) \iff a \parallel b
blocks.caption: Unlike Lamport clocks, both directions hold. The vector order is exactly the happened-before order.

scenes.caption: Cell (row, column) is 1 if the row event happened before the column event, -1 if the column event happened before the row event, 0 if they are concurrent (or the same event). Every value comes from comparing vectors.
a3 [3,0,0] vs b2 [2,2,0]: A's entry is larger in a3, B's entry is larger in b2. Neither vector is below the other, so the cell is 0: concurrent. Lamport gave 3 < 4 and could not tell.
a1 [1,0,0] is below c2 [2,2,2] in every entry, so a1 happened before c2. Row a1 is mostly 1: almost everything later depends on it, except a1 vs c1.
Row a3 is all 0 except against a1 and a2. a3 sent no messages, so nothing after it on other nodes could have seen it.

blocks.md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

That cost is why vector clocks appear where the set of writers is small, such as Dynamo-style *version vectors* kept per data item (the HLC paper cites Dynamo using them), and not as a cluster-wide timestamp. The HLC paper calls space proportional to the number of nodes prohibitive for large systems. Neither Lamport nor vector clocks relate to physical time, so you also cannot ask either one for "the state as of 10:00".

blocks.question: Event x has vector [3,0,0] and event y has [2,2,0]. What is their relation?
options: x happened before y, because 3 > 2
y happened before x, because its sum is larger
They are concurrent
They are the same event
blocks.explain: x is larger in A's entry and y is larger in B's entry, so neither vector is less than or equal to the other. Incomparable vectors mean concurrent events. Sums and single entries are not meaningful comparisons.

blocks.question: A service has 2,000 stateless frontends that all write to a shared database, and wants timestamps for snapshot reads. Why is a vector clock a poor fit?
options: Every timestamp and message would carry about 2,000 counters, and vectors still cannot express a physical time like 10:00
Vector clocks cannot be compared at all once there are more than 64 nodes
Vector clocks require synchronized physical clocks
Vector clocks only work with exactly three nodes
blocks.explain: Vector size grows with the number of participants, so each row version and each RPC would carry thousands of integers. Vector clocks also have no relation to wall time, so a snapshot "as of 10:00" is not expressible. This gap is what hybrid logical clocks target.

lessons.title: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time

blocks.md: The **naive algorithm** in the paper just mixes in the physical clock: on a send or local event $l := \max(l+1, pt)$, on receive $l := \max(l+1, l.m+1, pt)$. It satisfies requirements 1 and 2, but the paper shows $l - pt$ can grow without bound. The single number tries to be both "largest physical time seen" and "event counter", so whenever events arrive faster than the clock ticks, the +1s pile up and there is no safe moment to pull $l$ back down.

blocks.title: Naive hybrid clock drifts away from physical time

params.name: E
params.label: events per ms along the chain

scenes.caption: Simplified model: clocks perfectly synced, a message relayed through E events every millisecond with zero delay. With E = 1 the naive clock keeps up: each +1 is matched by the physical clock's tick.

With E = 3 every millisecond adds 3 to l but only 1 to pt, so l minus pt grows by 2 per ms: 20 ms after 10 ms (computed by simulation). It never comes back, because l cannot be reset without breaking causality.
HLC keeps l equal to the largest physical time seen (0 drift here). The extra events go into c, which climbs to E minus 1 within a millisecond and resets to 0 when pt advances.

blocks.md:
The fix is one level of indirection. HLC splits the timestamp into two parts:

- $l$: the largest physical time this node has heard of, from its own clock or from any message;
- $c$: a small counter that orders events that share the same $l$.

Timestamps compare **lexicographically**: $(l, c) < (l', c')$ if $l < l'$, or $l = l'$ and $c < c'$. Here is the algorithm from Figure 5 of the paper.

blocks.caption: HLC for one node (Kulkarni et al., Figure 5). pt is the node's physical clock reading; (lm, cm) is the timestamp carried by the message.

blocks.title: Node B receives m1 = (10, 0) while its clock reads 7

scenes.caption: B's state is (6, 0) from a local event at pt = 6. Message m1 arrives from A stamped (10, 0); B's physical clock reads 7 because A runs 3 ms ahead.
Remember the old l so we can tell where the new value came from.
l becomes the largest of B's own l, the message's l and B's physical clock: max(6, 10, 7) = 10. B adopts A's larger time instead of its own wall clock.
l came from the message only (10 equals lm, not l_old), so c = cm + 1 = 1. The receive is now (10, 1), strictly after the send's (10, 0).
Result (10, 1). A wall-clock stamp would have said 7, earlier than the send at 10. HLC keeps l within the clock skew of pt: 10 minus 7 = 3 ms.

blocks.title: HLC timestamps (l, c) across three nodes

scenes.caption: B has a local event at pt 6 and gets (6,0); C has one at pt 8 and gets (8,0). With nobody ahead of them, l simply equals the physical clock and c is 0.
A, whose clock is 3 ms ahead, sends m1 at pt 10 stamped (10,0). B receives it when its own clock reads 7 and stamps (10,1).
B's next events at pt 8 and 9 still see l = 10 ahead of pt, so l stays and c counts: (10,2), then (10,3) for the send of m2.
C receives m2 at pt 9. Its own l is 8, the message has l = 10, so C adopts 10 and sets c = 3 + 1: (10,4).
B's physical clock passes 10. At pt 11 the max is the physical clock, so l = 11 and c resets: (11,0). C does the same at pt 12: (12,0). Ties never pile up for long.

blocks.md:
The paper proves the properties that make this useful:

- **Theorem 1:** $e \to f \Rightarrow (l.e, c.e) < (l.f, c.f)$, so HLC can replace a Lamport clock.
- **Theorem 2:** $l.f \ge pt.f$ for every event.
- **Corollary 1:** $|l.f - pt.f| \le \epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is the clock synchronization bound. In the trace, the largest gap is 3 ms, exactly A's lead.
- **Corollary 3:** $c.f \le N(\epsilon + 1)$ for $N$ nodes, assuming the physical clock advances at least one unit between events on a node.
- **Corollary 4:** if every message takes long enough for every node's clock to advance by at least $d$, then $c \le \epsilon / d + 1$.

blocks.tex: l.f > pt.f \;\Rightarrow\; \exists g:\; g \to f \,\land\, pt.g = l.f
blocks.caption: Theorem 3: if l is ahead of the local clock, some causally earlier event really read that physical time. l is never invented.

blocks.prompt: B's state is (10, 2). It receives a message stamped (10, 5) while its physical clock reads 9. What is the new timestamp?
blocks.reveal: **(10, 6).** l = max(10, 10, 9) = 10, which equals both the old l and the message's l. That is the first branch: c = max(2, 5) + 1 = 6. Taking the max of both counters is what makes the receive later than both the previous local event (10, 2) and the send (10, 5).

blocks.md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

blocks.question: A node is at (10, 3). It performs a local event when its physical clock reads 11. What timestamp does the event get?
blocks.explain: l = max(10, 11) = 11, which differs from the old l, so c resets to 0: (11, 0). The reset is what keeps c bounded: as soon as the physical clock catches up with l, all accumulated ties are forgotten.

blocks.question: A node at (10, 3) receives a message stamped (8, 7) when its physical clock reads 9. What is the result?
blocks.explain: l = max(10, 8, 9) = 10 equals only the old l, so c = 3 + 1 = 4, giving (10, 4). The message's counter 7 is ignored because its l is smaller: (8, 7) is already less than (10, 3). Taking max(c, cm) + 1 here would be a bug that inflates c.

lessons.title: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty

blocks.md: The paper packs an HLC into the 64-bit NTP timestamp format. NTP time has 32 bits of seconds and 32 bits of fraction. HLC keeps only the top 48 bits of the physical time for $l$ (always rounding up), which leaves 16 fraction bits: a resolution of $2^{-16}$ s, about 15.3 microseconds. The remaining 16 bits hold $c$, enough for values up to 65535. Because $l$ comes first, comparing the packed integers compares $(l, c)$ lexicographically.

Is 16 bits enough for $c$? The bound $N(\epsilon + 1)$ from lesson 4 is a worst case. The authors measured real deployments on AWS with nodes messaging each other as fast as they could, which is the hardest case because short delays make many receives land on the same $l$.

blocks.title: How large c gets in practice (16 AWS nodes)

scenes.caption: From the HLC paper: 16 nodes in one AWS region sending to each other continuously, average NTP offset 16 ms. c = 0 for 66.96% of events and the largest value seen was 7.
Same setup after NTP converged to an average offset of 6 ms: c = 0 rises to 75.43%, and c of 0 or 1 covers 93.94% of events. c = 7 was not reported (shown as 0).

blocks.md:
In a WAN run across four AWS regions the paper reports $c = 0$ for about 95% of events and $c = 1$ for the rest: cross-region delays exceed the clock skew, so a message's $l$ is usually already in the receiver's past. In simulations, a **straggler** node held at the edge of the allowed skew reached $c$ up to 97 at that node only, without raising $c$ elsewhere.

For resilience the paper adds two local actions: ignore a message whose $l$ is too far ahead of the local clock (a likely corrupted sender), and if bounds are ever violated, reset $l$ and $c$ to $pt$ and 0.

**CockroachDB** uses HLC for every transaction timestamp. Its `Timestamp` holds an `int64` wall time in nanoseconds plus an `int32` logical counter. The gateway picks a transaction's timestamp from its HLC, every request carries the sender's HLC time, and receivers update their clocks with it. The code differs slightly from Figure 5: `Update` only takes the max and the next `Now` call does the increment, which yields the same ordering.

blocks.caption: Locking and clock-jump checks removed. UpdateAndCheckMaxOffset additionally rejects a remote wall time more than the max offset ahead of the local clock, the paper's ignore rule.

blocks.md: HLC alone cannot tell a node that a write stamped slightly in its future happened before a read started elsewhere. CockroachDB therefore assumes a **maximum clock offset**, 500 ms by default. A transaction with timestamp $ts$ treats any value stamped in $[ts,\ ts + \text{max offset}]$ as uncertain.

scenes.caption: Simplified numbers. T starts on a gateway whose HLC reads 1000. With the default max offset of 500 ms, its uncertainty interval is [1000, 1500]: a write stamped in that range might have happened before T started on a slower clock.
Key z has a version at 900, below T's timestamp. T simply reads it: it is definitely in T's past.
Key y has a version at 1600, above the interval's upper bound 1500. Even with maximal skew it was written after T began, so T ignores it.
Key x has a version at 1200, inside the interval. T cannot tell if it came first, so it performs an uncertainty restart: its timestamp moves just above 1200 and it will now see that value.
The upper bound stays at 1500, so the window shrank from 500 ms to 300 ms. Restarts are bounded by the interval, and the blog post says at most once per node.

blocks.md:
The bound must actually hold, so nodes compare clocks over RPC heartbeats. Per the docs, a node that finds its clock out of sync with at least half of the other nodes by 80% of the max offset (0.8 x 500 = 400 ms by default) shuts itself down.

Google **Spanner** takes the opposite trade. Its TrueTime API returns an interval with error bound $\epsilon$, which the Spanner paper reports as a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms, 4 ms most of the time. A leader waits out the uncertainty before making a commit visible, so the expected **commit wait** is at least $2\bar{\epsilon}$, about 8 ms. Spanner always delays writes; CockroachDB sometimes restarts reads.

HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

If clocks drift beyond the configured max offset, CockroachDB's docs warn that single-key linearizability between causally dependent transactions can be violated: a read can miss a write that finished before the read began (a stale read). HLC preserves the order it has seen, but it cannot fix a node whose clock is silently far behind. Run NTP or a similar time service and monitor the offset.

blocks.question: An operator lowers CockroachDB's max offset to 250 ms. Using the 80% rule, at what offset from at least half of the other nodes will a node shut itself down?
options: 250 ms
125 ms
200 ms
400 ms
blocks.explain: 0.8 x 250 = 200 ms. 400 ms is the threshold for the 500 ms default. A smaller max offset shrinks uncertainty windows (fewer restarts) but makes spurious self-termination more likely when clocks or networks wobble.

blocks.question: A CockroachDB transaction has timestamp 5000 ms with a 500 ms max offset. It reads key k, whose newest version is stamped 5300 ms. What happens?
options: It ignores the version because 5300 is after 5000
It performs an uncertainty restart with a timestamp just above 5300, keeping the 5500 upper bound
It aborts the other transaction that wrote the version
It waits 500 ms, as Spanner's commit wait would
blocks.explain: 5300 lies inside [5000, 5500], so the write may have happened before the transaction began on a node with a faster clock. CockroachDB bumps the read timestamp above 5300 so the value becomes visible, and the upper bound stays at 5500, so the window shrinks. Ignoring it could produce a stale read.

blocks.question: Why does the paper keep l and c in separate fields instead of using the naive single counter max(l+1, l.m+1, pt)?
options: To save space: two fields are smaller than one
So l can always be reset back to pt when the physical clock catches up, keeping l minus pt bounded, while c carries the tie-breaking
Because vector clocks require two fields
So c can track the number of nodes in the cluster
blocks.explain: In the naive version the +1s are mixed into the same number as physical time, so l can drift arbitrarily far ahead. Separating them lets HLC throw away the counter (c = 0) whenever pt or a message brings a new, larger l, which is what bounds both l minus pt and c.
